questions.q: Which of these requests is a query?
questions.explain: A query asks for information and changes nothing, so it is safe to retry and to cache. The other three change state, so they are commands.
options: order.cancel: cancel an order and release its stock
invoice.markPaid: record that an invoice was paid

questions.q: Why does a command have exactly one handler, while an event can have many listeners?
questions.explain: "Place this order" must be done once, by the code responsible for orders, and return its result. An event only announces a fact, so any number of listeners may react, and the publisher expects no answer.
options: Because handlers are slower than listeners
A command asks for one change and expects one answer; two handlers could both change state or disagree about the result
Because TypeScript cannot type more than one handler

questions.q: Checkout must know the new order id to show it on the receipt. Which message fits?
questions.explain: Checkout needs an answer from exactly one handler, and it is asking for a change. That is a command. After it succeeds, the handler can publish order.placed so e-mail and analytics react.
options: An event order.placed, reading the id from the first listener
A command order.place whose result type contains the order id
A query order.place, because it returns data
Either an event or a command; there is no difference

questions.q: Why does the lesson's Bus take the whole handler table in its constructor instead of offering register(name, handler)?
questions.explain: A mapped type with one required property per request name turns "every command has a handler" into something the compiler checks. A series of register calls is just statements; nothing tracks which names are covered.
options: Typed as Handlers<S>, a missing handler is a missing property, which is a compile error; with one-by-one calls the compiler cannot know whether every name was registered
So that handlers can be replaced at runtime

questions.q: The types guarantee a handler for every name. Why does execute still check Object.hasOwn(this.handlers, request.type) at runtime?
questions.explain: Types are erased. Anything that did not go through the compiler, or went around it, can send any name. Object.hasOwn also rejects names such as "toString" that plain indexing would find on the prototype.
options: It does not need to; the check is dead code
Requests can come from JavaScript callers, any or unchecked data, and a clear error is better than calling undefined or an inherited method like toString

questions.q: Why is the bus declared as Bus<S extends Specs<S>>, with type Specs<S> = { readonly [K in keyof S]: Spec }, rather than Bus<S extends Record<string, Spec>>?
questions.explain: The constraint says "whatever keys S has, each must be a Spec". It works for interfaces and type aliases alike, and still refuses an entry without a result.
options: The two are identical; it is a style choice
Interfaces have no index signature and are not assignable to Record<string, Spec>; the self-referencing constraint accepts them and still checks every property

questions.q: With "order.cancel": { input: { orderId: string; reason: string }; result: … }, what does a caller pass to execute?
questions.explain: RequestOf is { readonly type: K } & Readonly<input>: one flat object. K is inferred from its type field, and the other fields are checked against that request's input.

questions.q: Unlike the event bus, the command bus needs no cast to call the handler. Why?
questions.explain: The event bus stored listeners in a Map, whose value type cannot depend on the key. A mapped object type can: Handlers<S>[K] resolves to the handler for exactly K.
options: The handler table is a mapped type with one precisely typed property per name, and indexing it with K gives exactly Handler<S, K>

questions.q: Why is "out of stock" part of order.place's result type instead of a thrown error?
questions.explain: Expected business failures are data: the type lists them, and if (!result.ok) narrows to them. Bugs and outages are not expected; they throw and become a generic 500.
options: Throwing is not allowed in async functions
It is an expected outcome a user can cause; in the result union, callers are forced to handle it, and the HTTP layer can map every such failure to a status
Result types are faster than exceptions
So that the order is saved anyway

questions.q: What does const statusFor: Record<ErrorOf<ResultOf<ShopCommands, "order.place">>, number> guarantee?
questions.explain: ErrorOf pulls the error union out of the result, and Record requires a key for every member. Nothing checks that the numbers are sensible; that is what tests are for.
options: That each failure has a unique status code
That every failure the command can return has a status; adding a failure to the spec breaks the build until it gets one
That the status codes are valid HTTP codes

questions.q: Query handlers receive OrderReader = Pick<ReadonlyMap<string, OrderView>, "get" | "values">. What does this achieve?
questions.explain: Handing out a narrower type is a capability: code can only do what its type allows. It is a strong hint, not a proof, which is why architecture tests and reviews still matter.
options: It makes it impossible for any query to change data
A query handler that calls set or delete on its dependency does not compile, which prevents accidents, but a handler could still import the store directly or cast
It copies the orders so queries see a snapshot

questions.q: Why does a Middleware<ShopQueries> that returns cache.get(key) (typed unknown) fail to compile?
questions.explain: A generic function cannot invent a value of a type it knows nothing about. Middleware can pass results through, log them or throw, and a cache needs one cast that you justify (the key contains the query's type).
options: Because Map.get cannot be used in middleware
Inside the generic middleware the result type ResultOf<S, K> is unknown to it, so the only values it can return are those produced by next()
Because caching is not allowed for queries

questions.q: The middleware type is type Middleware<S> = <K extends RequestName<S>>(request: RequestOf<S, K>, next: …) => …. Why is K on the function rather than on the type alias?
questions.explain: A generic function type is chosen fresh at every call. The bus calls the same audit middleware with "order.place" and then with "order.cancel", and each time next() has the matching result type.
options: It is a mistake; both forms mean the same
So one middleware value works for every request name; Middleware<S, K> would be a middleware for one fixed request
Because type aliases cannot have two type parameters
To make middleware run in parallel

questions.q: In abstract class Request<TResult> { declare readonly __result: TResult; }, why is the __result property there?
questions.explain: An unused type parameter changes nothing about a type's shape. The phantom property makes the result type part of the structure, so execute<T>(request: Request<T>) can infer T.
options: The bus stores the result in it
TypeScript compares types by structure; without a property that uses TResult, Request<number> and Request<string> are the same type, and execute could not infer the result

questions.q: What does declare readonly __result: TResult; produce in the compiled JavaScript?
questions.explain: A declare field tells TypeScript "this property exists" without emitting any code, so instances do not even have the key. That is why it costs nothing at runtime.
options: Nothing: declare fields exist only for the type checker

questions.q: What is a real advantage of class-based requests over the spec map?
questions.explain: Classes are decentralised: each module owns its requests. The price is that exhaustiveness is lost (missing handlers are runtime errors) and routing by constructor breaks for plain objects from JSON.
options: A missing handler becomes a compile error
A module can add a new request by defining a class and registering its handler, without editing a central spec

questions.q: A class-based bus routes by request.constructor. A PlaceOrder instance is sent through a queue as JSON and parsed on the other side. What happens?
questions.explain: JSON has no classes. Anything that crosses a process boundary must carry a string discriminator, which is one reason the spec-map design uses a type field.
options: It is routed to the PlaceOrder handler as before
The parsed value is a plain object whose constructor is Object, so no handler is found unless the class is rebuilt from a type field

questions.q: With @zudojs/cqrs, await bus.execute<PlaceOrder, string>(command) compiles although the handler returns an object. What is the second type argument?
questions.explain: The bus stores handlers by runtime string, so at the call site it cannot know which handler will answer. The result type argument is taken on trust, like as. A typed layer that derives it from your spec makes it correct by construction.
options: A check against the registered handler's result
A claim: nothing connects it to what the handler returns
The type of the command's type field

questions.q: In @zudojs/cqrs, what is the type of await commands.execute(createCommand("order.place", payload)) with no type arguments?
questions.explain: execute<TCommand, TResult = void> falls back to void. That hides the result rather than lying about it; to use the value you must supply (or derive) the result type.
options: void, because the result type parameter defaults to void, even though the handler may return a value
The handler's return type, inferred from the registration

questions.q: A @zudojs/cqrs command bus has no handler for "order.refund". When do you find out?
questions.explain: Handlers are registered one call at a time, at runtime, so only the bus itself knows what is registered. Check completeness at startup, or register from a typed handler table.
options: At compile time, because createCommand checks registered names

questions.q: A customer double-clicks "Pay", and two identical invoice.pay commands arrive. What prevents a double charge?
questions.explain: Types describe one call; they cannot see that two valid calls are the same intent. Idempotency is a runtime design, usually a table of processed command ids written in the same transaction as the payment.
options: A command id recorded by the handler, so a repeated id returns the earlier result instead of charging again

questions.q: Why should commands return small results (an id, or a known failure) rather than the full updated order?
questions.explain: Separating the write result from the read model is the core of CQRS. A command that returns a full view couples every caller to the read shape and to the handler's timing.
options: It keeps commands cheap to retry and easy to move to a queue later; callers that need the full data send a query
So the handler does not need a database

questions.explain: handlers["toString"] finds Object.prototype.toString, so an attacker-chosen name runs a method you never registered. Called without a this in strict code, it returns "[object Undefined]". Object.hasOwn before the lookup closes the hole.
options:

no handler

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A declare field produces no JavaScript, so instances never have the key. The phantom property exists only for the type checker, which uses it to carry the result type.

questions.q: A command payload comes from a request body that tries to smuggle in a different type. What does this print?
questions.explain: createCommand lets its first argument win over a type key in the payload, so untrusted input cannot reroute the command, and it freezes the result. The type CommandOf encodes the same rule by omitting type from the payload.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type argument string is a claim that nothing checks, so the program compiles and fee is typed as a string. At runtime it is the number the handler returned. Calling a string method on it would crash.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The data survives the round trip, but the class does not: the parsed value is a plain object. The as PlaceOrder cast hides that from the compiler, and constructor-based routing finds no handler.

questions.q: This handler changes stock inside the loop that checks it. What does this print?
questions.explain: The rice was reserved before the oil check failed, so a refused order still took two bags. The lesson's handler checks every line first and changes stock only after all checks pass. No type can see this; a test that checks stock after a failed order can.

questions.q: Finish execute: if the handler table has no own property for request.type, throw Error('no handler for "NAME"'); otherwise call the handler and return its result. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Indexing the mapped handler table with K gives the handler for exactly that request, so no cast is needed. The Object.hasOwn check is for callers that went around the types, like the last line.

BUY RICE AND BEANS
true

questions.q: Write the "room.book" handler: refuse a nights value that is not a whole number of at least 1 ("invalid-nights"), refuse a room in taken ("room-taken"), otherwise mark the room taken and return { bookingId: "BK-" + roomId, totalKobo: nights * RATE_KOBO }. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: The handler table's type gives roomId and nights their types and checks every returned object against the result union, so a misspelled error such as "room-busy" would not compile. Validation comes before any change, so a refused booking leaves taken as it was.

questions.q: Finish pipeline: run the middleware in order, each receiving the request type and a next that runs the rest, and end with the handler. The program should print the five lines shown.
questions.explain: run(index) calls middleware number index with a next that is run(index + 1), and past the end calls the handler. The generic Middleware type means log works for any result type. When guard throws, log's "end" line never runs, because await next() rejected.
questions.expected:
start order.get
end order.get
ORD-7: placed
start admin.wipe
Error: admin.wipe needs an admin

questions.q: Derive the error union from TransferResult with a conditional type ErrorOf, map every error to a status code (insufficient-funds 422, account-frozen 423, same-account 400), and finish toHttp. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: ErrorOf distributes over the result union: the success member gives never, the failure member gives its error union. Record then demands a status for each error, so a new failure in the command's result breaks the build until it has one.

questions.q: Finish the class-based bus: register stores the handler under the request class, and execute looks it up by request.constructor, throwing Error("no handler for CLASSNAME") when there is none. The program should print ₦12500.00 and the error.
questions.explain: execute infers T from the phantom __result of the request's class, so kobo is a number. The one cast connects the loosely typed map to that result. A missing handler can only be found at runtime in this design.

questions.q: Write ask(type, input) over a @zudojs/cqrs query bus. The name must be a key of ShopQueries, the input and the result types must come from the spec, and the query object is built with createQuery. The program should print ₦75000 and RICE-50KG.
questions.explain: The package's result type argument is still a claim, but it is now derived from the same K as the name, inside one function, so callers can no longer get it wrong. Registering the raw handlers from a typed table, as the lesson did for commands, would make the other half safe too.

questions.q: Make payInvoice idempotent: if a command with the same commandId was already processed, return the earlier receipt without charging again. The program should print the four lines shown.
questions.explain: A retry of the same command returns the stored receipt; a new command id is a new intent and is charged. In production the processed ids live in the database and are written in the same transaction as the charge, so a crash between the two cannot leave them out of step.
questions.expected:
receipt 1: INV-9 ₦45000
receipt 1: INV-9 ₦45000
receipt 2: INV-9 ₦45000
charges: 2
